Why it matters: Lethal injection has been the dominant U.S. execution method for decades, accounting for roughly 89% of the 1,683 executions carried out since 1976, per the Death Penalty Information Center . Driving the news: Pike , convicted of killing a classmate three decades ago, survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs Wednesday in what would have been the state's first execution of a woman in 200 years. So in 1769, Frederick the Great landed on a novel strategy to keep money flowing into his borders. He organized cash-poor nobles into cooperatives, and began offering, to the highest bidders, bonds based on the value of their land. European investors snapped them up, giving Prussia the injection of cash it needed. articles.title: Nation Of Bondholders
articles.author: Michael Waters
articles.summary: It turns out you can trace America’s 2008 financial crash, in a roundabout way, to 18th-century Prussia. The Seven Years’ War left the kingdom in financial shambles: Just to afford the fighting, Prussia’s king, Frederick the Great, had hired private minters to ramp up currency production . So in 1769, Frederick the Great landed on a novel strategy to keep money flowing into his borders. He organized cash-poor nobles into cooperatives, and began offering, to the highest bidders, bonds based on the value of their land. European investors snapped them up, giving Prussia the injection of cash it needed. It was, as the journalist Robin Wigglesworth writes in his new book, A Fabulous Debt: The Epic History of How Bonds Built the Modern World , possibly the world’s first mortgage bond sale. A Fabulous Debt is a rollicking look at the development of the bond market, perhaps the least appreciated—but, Wigglesworth convincingly argues, the most important—financial market in the world today. Wigglesworth connects overzealous use of bonds both to the Great Recession and to America’s massive ballooning $40 trillion national debt. Paired with another recent book, David I. articles.title: Trump tightens chokehold on Cuba
articles.author: Shelby Talcott
articles.summary: The Trump administration is still eyeing Cuba, tightening travel rules and imposing new restrictions on banking this week in an effort to continue to squeeze the country’s regime. For many in the administration, the strategy toward Cuba remains simple: Wait until it falls. “Watch what he does with Cuba,” President Donald Trump recently quipped at the White House while introducing Secretary of State Marco Rubio. It remains to be seen whether that will be enough for Florida Republicans interested in regime change, but don’t be surprised if the US government imposes more restrictions. “The root of Cuba’s issues remains the dictatorship’s blatant kleptocracy and economic mismanagement,” a State Department spokeswoman said. “For a safer and more prosperous hemisphere, we consider all options that will drive economic and political reforms to give the Cuban people a better future.” — Shelby Talcott
